passage: Sonali was showing photos from the Class 10 trip when she pointed at Jahnavi. "You people from your state are all loud and never on time, aren't you?" A few classmates laughed. Jahnavi felt like a photo cropped down to one corner. Jahnavi had been on time every day that week and was quiet in most classes. "That isn't me," Jahnavi said, "and it isn't everyone from home either. My cousin is the quietest person I know." Sonali blinked. "Oh. I just heard it somewhere." At lunch Riya sat beside Jahnavi and said, "Glad you spoke up." For the first time that week Jahnavi's shoulders dropped.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi answer when the label was made?
qa.a: Jahnavi said, That isn't me, and it isn't everyone from home either.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when Sonali pointed, and what does the photo image show?
qa.a: Unseen and reduced; feeling like a photo cropped to one corner shows being seen as one label instead of a whole person.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi afterwards?
qa.a: Correcting the label calmly with a personal example, and Riya sitting beside Jahnavi at lunch.

qa.q: Why might Sonali have made the remark?
qa.a: Sonali had heard it somewhere and repeated it without thinking; the surprised blink suggests it was borrowed, not personal.

grounding: A teenager is told all people from their state are a certain way, feels unseen, and gently corrects it with supportive peers.

passage:
At the hockey club after practice, in the changing area:
Swati: You're from that community, right? Everyone from there is stingy.
Rashmi: Sorry? Say that again?
Swati: I mean, that's just what people say.
Rashmi: I bought the whole team samosas last week. And my grandfather runs a free water stall every summer.
Swati: Okay, but that's you.
Rashmi: Exactly. It's me. Do you want to know me, or the label?
Swati: ...Fair. I'm sorry.
Neha, who had been lacing shoes on the bench, looked up. "Rashmi, sit with me at lunch tomorrow?"
Rashmi: Thanks, Neha. I'd like that.

qa.q: What did Rashmi buy for the whole team last week?
qa.a: Rashmi bought samosas for the whole team.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel on hearing that everyone from there is stingy?
qa.a: Hurt and unseen, and a little angry; Rashmi asked Swati to say it again and answered with facts about Rashmi's own life.

qa.q: What worked in how Rashmi answered?
qa.a: Personal examples and the question of whether Swati wanted to know Rashmi or the label, without attacking.

qa.q: What might Neha's invitation to lunch mean to Rashmi?
qa.a: That Rashmi is not alone, which helps a person feel seen.

grounding: A teenager is told everyone from their community is stingy, feels unseen, and answers with personal examples and finds support.

passage:
On the first day of the inter-school debate camp in Pune, the coordinator read out team roles. "Usha, you're from Punjab, so you'll be our loud one. Opening speaker!" A few students laughed. Usha felt her ears burn. She was the quietest person in her family; she liked writing rebuttals, not shouting openings. Later a boy at lunch said, "Punjabis only eat butter chicken, na?" She had been vegetarian since she was nine. She pushed her dal around and felt invisible, a label walking around with her face.
In the evening session, Rekha, a girl from Kochi, sat beside her. "They told me I must be good at maths because I'm from Kerala. I'm terrible." Usha laughed for the first time that day. Together they went to the coordinator. Usha said politely, "I'd like to try rebuttals. I'm not very loud." The coordinator paused, then nodded. "Fair. Rebuttals it is."

qa.q: Which role did Usha ask to try?
qa.a: Rebuttals.

qa.q: How did Usha feel after the lunch comment?
qa.a: She felt unseen and invisible, like a label walking around with her face, pushing her dal around.

qa.q: What helped Usha, and why?
qa.a: Finding Rekha, who had faced the same thing, gave her support, and together they gently corrected the coordinator by asking for the role that fitted her.

qa.q: How might the coordinator have seen the moment when Usha asked?
qa.a: The coordinator may have been surprised and a little embarrassed at the assumption, and then open to treating Usha as an individual.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reduced to a regional label who feels unseen, and finds a supportive peer and gently corrects it.

passage:
Dear Yamini didi,
Three weeks at the new school in Delhi. You asked how it is, so here's the truth. On day one, Rohan said, "You're Gujarati, so you'll be selling us something, right?" and everyone laughed. Since then, every time I bring thepla, it's "the Gujju tiffin". The teacher asked me to do the class accounts "because you people are good at business." I'm not. I'm good at drawing. I felt like nobody even knew my name, just my state.
Last Friday I tried something. When Rohan said it again, I said, "My dad's a teacher and I can't add. Try another joke." It came out calm, somehow. A few people laughed with me, not at me. And a boy called Imran said he's tired of "all Biharis are like this" jokes too. We sat together at lunch. He draws comics.
Write back soon.
Darshan

qa.q: What is Darshan actually good at?
qa.a: Darshan is good at drawing.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel in the first weeks, and why?
qa.a: Darshan felt unseen and frustrated, as if nobody knew Darshan's name, only Darshan's state, because of the jokes and assumptions.

qa.q: What did Darshan do that helped?
qa.a: Darshan corrected Rohan calmly with a light, true reply, and then found a supportive peer in Imran who faced similar jokes.

qa.q: How might Imran see the jokes in class?
qa.a: Imran is tired of being labelled too, and probably felt relief finding someone who understood.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager treated as a state stereotype who feels unseen, gently corrects it and finds a supportive peer.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Ira, thanks for having me on the school podcast. So, I'm Farhan, sixteen, and when we moved to Bengaluru from the old city in Hyderabad, the first thing a classmate said was, "People from your side of town are all hot-headed, na?" Like a joke. But then every time I spoke up in class, someone would say, "Here comes the temper." I stopped speaking up. I just wanted them to see me, not a map. What changed? Two things. First, I said once, quite calmly, "I'm actually the calmest one in my family. Ask my mum." People laughed, but it stuck. Second, I joined the robotics club, and there nobody cared where I came from, just whether my code worked. My friends there call me Farhan, not Hyderabad. That made the difference.

qa.q: What did the robotics club care about?
qa.a: Just whether Farhan's code worked.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when classmates said "Here comes the temper"?
qa.a: Farhan felt unseen and discouraged, so Farhan stopped speaking up in class.

qa.q: Which of Farhan's two steps would you advise another new student to try first?
qa.a: A calm, gentle correction like Farhan's, because it challenges the label without a fight, and then looking for a group like the robotics club where people judge you by what you do.

qa.q: How might Ira react to Farhan's story as the host?
qa.a: Ira might feel sympathetic and curious, perhaps recognising the same kinds of jokes from their own school.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reduced to a label about their area who feels unseen, gently corrects it and finds supportive peers.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
Day one of the chemistry project, Rohan grinned at Charu. "You're from Patna, so you'll just mug up the answers, na? All Biharis do." The others laughed. Charu laughed too, then spent the bus ride home staring at her own reflection in the window, feeling like a word instead of a person.
Three days later, the group divided tasks. Rohan handed her note-taking again. Charu's hands shook, but she said, "I'm actually good at the experiment part. I built the working model at my old school." Rohan shrugged. "Okay, okay, sorry." It sounded thin.
The next week, Deepika saved her a seat in the lab. "Your titration was the cleanest in the class," she said. "Want to prepare for the practical exam together?" Charu nodded, and for the first time since moving to Pune, she talked through the whole period.

qa.q: Which city is Charu from?
qa.a: Charu is from Patna.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling on the bus ride home after the first day?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unseen, like a word instead of a person, even though she had laughed along in the group.

qa.q: What helped Charu stop being boxed in by the label?
qa.a: Gently correcting Rohan by naming her real strength, and then finding a supportive classmate in Deepika, who noticed her actual work.

qa.q: How does Deepika see Charu, compared with Rohan?
qa.a: Deepika sees her as an individual with skills, praising her clean titration, while Rohan saw only where she came from.

grounding: Shows a teenager labelled by her home state, feeling unseen, then gently correcting it and finding a supportive peer.
